patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Iain Wares: Edinburgh → South Africa; Birmingham → California: Fr James Robinson; Scotland → Toronto: Fr Paul Moore; Fort Augustus → Australia: Denis Chrysostom Alexander; England → Zimbabwe (John Smyth 'exported to Africa').
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, brother, teacher or headmistress was found abusing children, the institution often moved them rather than calling the police: to another parish, another school, another state, or another continent. The map draws 34 documented moves recorded by inquiries, courts and the institutions' own files, and colors every country that sent or received an abuser. The Pennsylvania grand jury found bishops moved abusers between parishes; Bishop Mulkearns knew of Gerald Ridsdale's offending by late 1975 and kept reappointing him to new parishes; the Adass Israel School paid for Malka Leifer's 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel before police were told; the Makin review called John Smyth "a problem solved and exported to Africa".

patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases the sources date both the first complaint that reached police, a church, an employer or officials, and the first conviction, charge or official finding. The middle wait is 12.0 years. A pupil told police about the MP Cyril Smith in 1968 and was told Smith was "a very important, powerful man"; in 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged and had been assured in 1970 that he would not be. Complaints about Jimmy Savile reached police from 1958; investigations in his lifetime brought no charges. Athletes complained about Larry Nassar from 1997. Each country is colored by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role_note: Scotland 2017: Limitation (Childhood Abuse) (Scotland) Act 2017 removed the three-year time bar for childhood abuse civil claims (announced in force 4 Oct 2017) England and Wales 2026: Crime and Policing Act 2026 s.96 removed the three-year limitation period for child sexual abuse personal-injury claims, retrospectively; in force 29 June 2026; defendants must show a fair trial is impossible
patterns.pattern_summary: Most survivors disclose decades later, after the legal deadline to sue or prosecute has passed. Where legislatures tried to lift those deadlines, the institutions facing claims lobbied against it, and when the deadlines fell, many filed for bankruptcy. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018; in Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Catholic Conference spent over $7.6 million and the insurance federation nearly $20.7 million from 2014 to 2024. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and orders filed for bankruptcy, several within hours or days of a trial, a deposition or a new law.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2014: Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (IICSA), England and Wales; announced 7 July 2014, statutory from Feb 2015, final report 20 Oct 2022. 19 reports; Catholic Church report (Nov 2020) found it put reputation before children; first final recommendation fully implemented only in June 2026 (limitation reform)
patterns.pattern_summary: Official inquiries into institutional child abuse came in waves: Canada and Ireland first (Hughes, 1989; the Ryan commission, 1999–2009), the United States in 2002–2004, most of western Europe after 2010, Australia's Royal Commission 2013–2017, then France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland from 2021. Where inquiries used population surveys, the numbers were far above church records: about 216,000 minors abused by French clergy and religious since 1950, against about 3,000 identified before. Many "national" studies were commissioned by the church itself. Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, with some of the largest Catholic populations, have no national inquiry in the sources reached.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Holy See and IICSA (England & Wales): —
patterns.pattern_summary: When the accused belongs to another state, a diplomatic service or an army, prosecution depends on that state. UN peacekeepers fall under their own country's courts: at least 134 Sri Lankan soldiers were accused of abusing nine Haitian children in 2004–2007 and none was convicted. The Holy See recalled its nuncio to the Dominican Republic, Józef Wesołowski, and told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow his extradition. South Korea's court refused to send the Welcome to Video operator to the United States. Morocco's king pardoned a Spanish child rapist as a gesture to Spain. Israel's deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments that kept Malka Leifer from extradition for years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 1 documented adoption flows into United Kingdom on this map.
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption moved from one sending country to the next as each was exposed. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad from 1953 to 2008; its Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in 2025 that the state was responsible for human rights violations in those adoptions. Romania (1990s), Guatemala (until 2007–08), Cambodia and Vietnam, Nepal, Ethiopia (banned 2018) and others followed, each closed after inquiries found children bought, stolen or registered as orphans. Receiving countries then began to look at themselves: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after the Joustra committee, and China ended it in 2024. The map colors each sending country by whether it was later closed or suspended and draws 59 documented flows.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: British child migration programmes — IICSA. United Kingdom — forced adoption of unmarried mothers' babies 1949–1976 (JCHR 2022; apology 2026).
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children were carried out by states, as policy. Argentina's junta took about 500 babies from detained mothers in 1976–83 (a 2012 court found a "systematic plan"; 140 grandchildren had been identified by July 2025). Under Franco, children were taken from Republican and later unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children into residential schools and non-Indigenous families; Denmark sent Greenlandic children to Danish families in 1951; France moved children from Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported Ukrainian children; the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants in March 2023 for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over it.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 2003: Sexual Offences Act 2003 allows prosecution in England, Wales and NI of offences against children abroad (Scotland: 1995 Act); used to convict Richard Huckle in 2016 2019: Europol IOCTA 2019: live distant child abuse (LDCA) is the most common form of commercial child sexual exploitation; the Philippines remains the most prominent victim location; some offenders also travel; EU police urged to use PNR travel data
patterns.pattern_summary: Child sex tourism followed enforcement around the map. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. When Manila closed Ermita in 1992, businesses moved to Angeles City. Offenders' home countries passed laws to prosecute their citizens for abuse abroad (Germany 1993, Australia 1994, Canada 1997, Japan 1999, the US PROTECT Act 2003). Then the trade moved online: in the Philippines, street and establishment child sex trafficking fell 79–86% in targeted cities (2006–2016), while monthly Philippine internet addresses used for child sexual exploitation rose more than twelvefold (2014–2017).

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role_note: Kincora Boys' Home (Belfast) — claims of MI5/army intelligence complicity (investigated and disproved). Elm Guest House, London — VIP-abuse claims (investigated and disproved). Operation Midland — Carl Beech's false 'VIP ring' claims (investigated and disproved).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect child-abuse networks are common. The records sort them into what was proven, what was disproved and what is still only claimed. Proven: the founder of Colonia Dignidad in Chile was convicted of abusing children there and charged with aiding the Pinochet regime, which Chilean officials say used the colony to torture opponents, and Germany admitted its embassy looked away. West Berlin's youth authorities placed boys with men known to be paedophiles as foster fathers, from the late 1960s, on a psychologist's advice. US troops in Afghanistan were told not to intervene when allied commanders abused boys. UN police monitors and US contractors in Bosnia bought trafficked girls. The FBI and Australian police ran abuse sites for weeks to months to identify users. Disproved: the Kincora inquiry found no evidence MI5 used the home for blackmail; the Met's Operation Midland "VIP ring" was invented by a man later jailed for it. Claimed, not established: that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role_note: United Kingdom → Philippines demand for livestreamed abuse.
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse runs on ordinary infrastructure: hosting companies, payment systems and the largest social platforms. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation found most of the abuse material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports to the US CyberTipline rose from 4,560 in 1998 to over 36 million in 2023, then fell after Meta encrypted its messages, not because abuse fell. Payments for livestreamed abuse run from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines; Australia's Westpac agreed a A$1.3 billion penalty in 2020 that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. Backpage earned more than $500 million from ads used to sell children before it was shut in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: United Kingdom — forced adoption of unmarried mothers' babies 1949–1976 (JCHR 2022; apology 2026); North Wales children's homes — Waterhouse Inquiry 'Lost in Care'; Kincora Boys' Home, Belfast — Hart Inquiry findings; Lambeth Council children's homes (Shirley Oaks, South Vale, Angell Road) — IICSA; Nottinghamshire and Nottingham councils (incl. Beechwood) — IICSA; Medomsley Detention Centre, County Durham — Neville Husband and staff; Islington Council children's homes, London; Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse — final report (England and Wales); British child migration programmes — IICSA; Jimmy Savile — 'Giving Victims a Voice' (Met Police/NSPCC); Lampard report — Savile in NHS hospitals; Cyril Smith MP — Cambridge House and Knowl View, Rochdale; IICSA Westminster report — deference and failures (no proven 'VIP ring'); Lord Greville Janner — allegations from Leicestershire chil.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 242 cases on this map, police, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part, or a court or inquiry found they ignored, buried or obstructed it. In Rotherham the Jay report found about 1,400 children exploited from 1997 to 2013 and called the council's and police's failures "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. A senior Australian police officer in 1972 offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. North Wales police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, Puebla police arrested the journalist who exposed a Cancún abuse ring, and leaked calls recorded the state governor discussing her jailing; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

patterns.pattern: False alarms that drown real cases
patterns.role_note: Kincora Boys' Home (Belfast) — claims of MI5/army intelligence complicity. Elm Guest House, London — VIP-abuse claims. Operation Midland — Carl Beech's false 'VIP ring' claims.
patterns.pattern_summary: Invented trafficking stories take resources from real ones. In July 2020 the US National Human Trafficking Hotline received hundreds of reports about a false claim that the furniture seller Wayfair was selling children; the hotline's operator, Polaris, said the volume made it harder to help people who needed it, and none of the reports had new information. "Pizzagate" led to a man firing a rifle inside a Washington restaurant in 2016. London's Metropolitan Police spent over £2 million on Operation Midland, built on a "VIP ring" story invented by Carl Beech, who was himself jailed for child-abuse offences. The McMartin preschool trials in the 1980s cost about $15 million and ended without a conviction.

cases.title: John Smyth — Iwerne camps, Zimbabwe and South Africa (Makin Review)
cases.who: Iwerne Trust (evangelical camps), Church of England; Zambesi Ministries (Zimbabwe); Anglican Church of Southern Africa
cases.what: John Smyth QC, chair of the Iwerne Trust 1974–81, beat and abused boys and young men he met through the evangelical Iwerne camps and Winchester College's Christian Forum. After the 1982 Ruston Report he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, founding Zambesi Ministries camps for boys in 1986; a 16-year-old died at one of his camps in December 1992 and Smyth was arrested in 1997 but never charged anywhere. Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, he moved to South Africa in 2001 and the review found abuse likely continued until his death in Cape Town on 11 August 2018. Keith Makin's review was published on 7 November 2024; Archbishop Justin Welby resigned on 12 November 2024.
cases.cover_up: A 1982 internal Iwerne Trust report (the Ruston Report) described the beatings; the Makin Review found an 'active cover-up' by its recipients; police were not told until 2013. The review called Smyth 'a problem solved and exported to Africa' and found no evidence of proactive attempts to alert Zimbabwean authorities.

cases.title: Romania–UK 'loverboy' network dismantled — 21 arrested (Eurojust, 2020)
cases.who: Romanian organized criminal group using the 'loverboy' method
cases.what: On 9 September 2020 a Romanian–UK Joint Investigation Team supported by Eurojust arrested 21 members of a hierarchical group active since 2009 that seduced vulnerable Romanian girls with false promises of relationships, exploited minors in prostitution in Romania until they turned 18, and then moved them to the UK, Ireland and Germany. Thirty-two house searches were carried out (23 in Romania, 9 in the UK). Eurojust said Romania and the UK had cooperated in 76 trafficking investigations in four years.

cases.title: Fr Brendan Smyth — Norbertine order
cases.who: Norbertine order (Kilnacrott Abbey); Fr Brendan Smyth
cases.what: Norbertine priest Brendan Smyth abused children for decades from the 1950s in Northern Ireland, the Republic and the United States; the BBC put the number at at least 143. In 1975 Seán Brady, later Cardinal, attended church meetings where two teenage victims were sworn to secrecy; their evidence was never given to police. The Irish government's delay in acting on the RUC's extradition request led to the collapse of the Reynolds coalition in 1994. He was jailed in Northern Ireland in 1994 for abusing dozens of children there, and in July 1997 was sentenced in Dublin to 12 years for abusing 20 children in the Republic. He died in the Curragh Prison in August 1997. The Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry (2017) found the Norbertine order moved him to another diocese despite knowing his history.
cases.cover_up: Norbertines moved him between parishes, dioceses and countries without reporting him; at a 1975 church inquiry two boys signed oaths of silence; mishandled extradition by the Irish Attorney General's office contributed to the fall of the government in 1994

cases.title: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
cases.who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
cases.what: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Sri Lanka changed its rules after a 1987 police raid found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions'.
cases.cover_up: Adoption records were widely falsified; 'acting mothers' were paid to pose as birth mothers in court.

cases.title: Terry Knight — Diocese of Portsmouth
cases.who: Church of England, Diocese of Portsmouth
cases.what: Terry Knight, active in the Diocese of Portsmouth, was convicted of child sexual offences in 1996 and again in 2016. Parents had raised concerns with the bishop in 1985, who did not inform police.
cases.cover_up: Bishop Timothy Bavin did not report Knight to police when parents raised concerns in 1985.

cases.title: Medomsley Detention Centre, County Durham — Neville Husband and staff
cases.who: Medomsley Detention Centre for young offenders (Home Office Prison Service)
cases.what: Medomsley held young male offenders from 1961 to 1988. Neville Husband, an officer who ran the kitchens, was convicted of sexual offences in 2003 and again in 2005 and died in 2010; the Ombudsman called him 'possibly the most prolific sex offender in British history'. Operation Seabrook (from 2013) identified 32 living suspects; five former officers were convicted in 2019 and another in 2023, eight former staff jailed in total. The Ombudsman's report of 12 November 2025, based on 8,000 documents and 74 witnesses, found the authorities failed in their duty to keep detainees safe.
cases.cover_up: The Prisons and Probation Ombudsman (November 2025) found that knowledge of the abuse held by the Prison Service, police and Home Office was 'ignored and dismissed', families' complaints led to no action, and successive wardens were 'either complicit or incompetent'.

cases.title: Islington Council children's homes, London
cases.who: London Borough of Islington children's homes and foster placements (42 homes)
cases.what: Survivors say children in Islington's 42 children's homes and in foster care were abused between the 1960s and 1990s; the Evening Standard exposed abuse in the homes in 1992. A 2018 independent report by Sarah Morgan QC into former councillor Sandy Marks found evidence linking her to the 'Fallen Angels' group (which she denies) but no evidence it affected her council duties or that she learned of organised abuse. Islington later set up a support payment scheme for survivors.
cases.cover_up: A 2018 report by Sarah Morgan QC found that councillor Sandy Marks knew of abuse allegations before the Evening Standard published them in 1992; the council leadership publicly denied the newspaper's reports at the time.

cases.title: Kendall House girls' home, Gravesend — Proctor review
cases.who: Kendall House, a Church of England children's home taking girls placed by social services
cases.what: An independent review chaired by Dr Sue Proctor, commissioned by the Bishop of Rochester and published in July 2016, found that from 1967 girls as young as 11 were routinely given antidepressants, sedatives and antipsychotics, sometimes without medical assessment. Former residents were physically, emotionally and sometimes sexually abused, including two rapes while girls were held in isolation. The review heard from 20 former residents and examined records of 44. A 1980 television programme had already exposed the home.

cases.title: Ghislaine Maxwell — convicted of sex trafficking of a minor
cases.who: Ghislaine Maxwell
cases.what: Maxwell was arrested on 2 July 2020 in Bradford, New Hampshire. On 29 December 2021 a jury convicted her on five of six counts, including sex trafficking of a minor; she was acquitted of enticing a minor to travel. She was sentenced on 28 June 2022 to 20 years. The Second Circuit upheld the conviction on 17 Sept 2024 and the US Supreme Court declined her appeal on 6 Oct 2025; she had argued Epstein's 2007 non-prosecution agreement shielded co-conspirators. As of mid-2026 her lawyer said he would seek a pardon; Blanche said in May 2026 he would not recommend one.
cases.cover_up: In July 2025 Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche interviewed Maxwell with limited immunity; on 1 Aug 2025 she was moved to the minimum-security Federal Prison Camp Bryan, Texas. A DOJ official recorded secretly said the transfer was against policy (DOJ said he had no role).

cases.title: Jimmy Savile — 'Giving Victims a Voice' (Met Police/NSPCC)
cases.who: Jimmy Savile (BBC broadcaster); BBC; NHS hospitals; Metropolitan Police
cases.what: After Savile's death in October 2011, an ITV documentary, 'Exposure: The Other Side of Jimmy Savile', broadcast on 3 Oct 2012, carried accounts of abuse of under-age teenage girls. The Metropolitan Police opened a criminal investigation, Operation Yewtree, on 19 Oct 2012. The January 2013 Met/NSPCC report 'Giving Victims a Voice' recorded 214 crimes across 28 police force areas, including 34 rape or penetration offences, from 1955 to 2009; 450 people had made allegations against him, 73% of them under 18 at the time. The CPS apologised for missing the chance to prosecute him in 2009. The report found no clear evidence that he operated in a paedophile ring.
cases.cover_up: Earliest known police report dates from 1958, with police intelligence from 1963; Surrey Police investigated in 2007–09 without charges. A BBC Newsnight investigation was shelved in December 2011; the Pollard Review called the decision flawed.

cases.title: Rochdale — Operation Span convictions and 2024 review
cases.who: Grooming network linked to two takeaway restaurants; Greater Manchester Police; Rochdale Council
cases.what: In May 2012 nine men were convicted after Operation Span, which Greater Manchester Police began in December 2010, more than two years after it was first told of abuse linked to two takeaways. Girls as young as 12 were plied with drink and drugs and passed between men for cash. A 173-page review published 15 January 2024 found children were 'left at the mercy' of gangs between 2004 and 2013 through a 'lamentable strategic failure' of senior police and council leaders; it identified hundreds of potential victims, mainly white girls from poor backgrounds, abused by Asian men, and said 96 men were still a potential risk to children.
cases.cover_up: Police identified ring-leaders in 2007 but did not pursue them; Operation Span launched over two years after the first reports.

cases.title: Cyril Smith MP — Cambridge House and Knowl View, Rochdale
cases.who: Cyril Smith (Liberal MP for Rochdale 1972–1992); Lancashire Constabulary; Director of Public Prosecutions; Rochdale Council
cases.what: Cyril Smith, Liberal MP for Rochdale 1972–1992, was alleged by eight men to have indecently assaulted them as teenagers in about 1961–1966; six had lived at Cambridge House hostel, which he helped set up. The Director of Public Prosecutions advised against prosecution in 1970, and CPS reviews in 1998 and 1999 did not lead to charges. He died on 3 September 2010, never charged. On 27 November 2012 Greater Manchester Police said the boys had been victims of physical and sexual abuse by Smith, and the CPS said he should have been charged. The IICSA report on Cambridge House, Knowl View and Rochdale (April 2018) found no evidence of improper influence on the DPP but said valuable opportunities to prosecute were lost in 1998 and 1999, and that discussions before his 1988 knighthood showed 'considerable deference to power'; witnesses also told it Smith assaulted boys at Knowl View School.
cases.cover_up: Police evidence presented in 1970 led to no action; the CPS said in 2012 that Smith should have been charged and that he had been given an assurance in 1970 he would not be prosecuted. Press allegations in 1979 (Rochdale Alternative Press, Private Eye) produced no prosecution. He was knighted in 1988 though Margaret Thatcher had been told of the allegations.

cases.title: Bishop Peter Ball — conviction and Church collusion
cases.who: Church of England; 'Give a Year to God' scheme
cases.what: Peter Ball, former Bishop of Lewes and of Gloucester, ran a 'Give a Year to God' scheme for young men that the Church did not monitor. Gloucestershire police investigated in 1992 and he accepted a caution for one offence; IICSA found the Crown Prosecution Service advice to caution was wrong and other charges were possible. He pleaded guilty in 2015 and on 7 October 2015 was jailed for 32 months for offences against 18 young men over 15 years. Dame Moira Gibb's review 'An Abuse of Faith' (June 2017) found the Church colluded with Ball; Lord Carey stepped back from ministry. IICSA also noted the Duchy of Cornwall bought a property rented to Ball and his brother.
cases.cover_up: Lambeth Palace received seven letters supporting complainant Neil Todd's allegations in 1992 but passed only the least incriminating one to police; Archbishop George Carey wrote to the Gloucestershire Chief Constable; Ball's twin brother, also a bishop, phoned potential complainants to dissuade them; Ball accepted a caution in 1992 and was soon returned to ministry, including work in schools.

cases.title: Barry Bennell and English youth football (Sheldon Review)
cases.who: Barry Bennell (coach/scout, Crewe Alexandra, Manchester City links); The Football Association
cases.what: Bennell was first jailed in Florida in 1994 for raping a British boy on a football tour, then received prison sentences in Britain in 1998, 2015, February 2018 (50 offences against 12 boys aged eight to 14, 1979–1990; 30 years) and October 2020 (a fifth sentence, making 34 years in total). After a former player spoke out publicly in November 2016, BBC News reported within weeks that 350 people had alleged they were victims, linked to 55 clubs. Clive Sheldon QC's review for the FA (17 Mar 2021) recorded at least 240 suspects and 692 survivors across football, said the true numbers were likely far higher, found the FA had acted 'far too slowly' on child protection, and criticised Manchester City, Crewe and Stoke over Bennell. Bennell died in prison in September 2023.
cases.cover_up: Crewe Alexandra heard an allegation but kept Bennell on with restrictions (former director Hamilton Smith). The Sheldon Review found the FA guilty of 'institutional failure' for delaying safeguards after 1995.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 12,511 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman). 2001: scandal: Andhra Pradesh adoption racket (Tender Loving Care Home) exposed, March 2001 2005: ban: Andhra Pradesh bars private agencies from placing children; 10 convicted (31 August) 2005: scandal: Chennai police arrest 9 over Malaysian Social Services kidnapping-for-adoption case (May) 2008: freeze: Australia freezes adoptions through Indian agencies whose conduct was in doubt (2 September)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption moved from one sending country to the next as each was exposed. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad from 1953 to 2008; its Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in 2025 that the state was responsible for human rights violations in those adoptions. Romania (1990s), Guatemala (until 2007–08), Cambodia and Vietnam, Nepal, Ethiopia (banned 2018) and others followed, each closed after inquiries found children bought, stolen or registered as orphans. Receiving countries then began to look at themselves: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after the Joustra committee, and China ended it in 2024. The map colors each sending country by whether it was later closed or suspended and draws 59 documented flows.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: India — Preet Mandir, Pune: CBI case on inter-country adoption racket; Muzaffarpur shelter home — TISS audit and convictions; TISS 'Koshish' social audit of 110 Bihar children's homes; Deoria shelter home, Uttar Pradesh — girls rescued, CBI case; Unnao rape case — MLA Kuldeep Singh Sengar; India — Kerala priest given double life (Kottapuram diocese).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 242 cases on this map, police, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part, or a court or inquiry found they ignored, buried or obstructed it. In Rotherham the Jay report found about 1,400 children exploited from 1997 to 2013 and called the council's and police's failures "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. A senior Australian police officer in 1972 offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. North Wales police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, Puebla police arrested the journalist who exposed a Cancún abuse ring, and leaked calls recorded the state governor discussing her jailing; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found South Asia lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation. Scholars note allegations "often remain informal and rarely progress to formal charges" (Matthew N. Schmalz)
patterns.pattern_summary: The map's documented record is thickest where people looked. Childlight's 2026 update rests on representative surveys from only 60 countries; South Asia, West and Central Africa and the Middle East and North Africa lack them. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied 2023 data. In 2025, 14% of the 23.4 million reports to the US CyberTipline could not be placed in any country, and North Korea had 12. Countries with large churches and many children's institutions, such as Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, have held no national inquiry into institutional abuse in the sources reached. Where a country is colored only by estimate on this map, this is why.

cases.title: Fr Joseph Jeyapaul — Indian priest extradited to Minnesota
cases.who: Diocese of Crookston, Minnesota; diocese in India
cases.what: An Indian priest serving in the Diocese of Crookston in 2004–2005 was removed from ministry in September 2005 and returned to India. He was charged in 2006 with raping a girl from age 14; extradition took about five years after an Interpol alert, with arrest in Erode, India in 2012 and return to Minnesota in November 2014. In 2015 he pleaded guilty to criminal sexual misconduct involving a teenage girl and was sentenced to a year and a day (time served); the rape charges were dismissed under the plea deal and he faced deportation to India.
cases.cover_up: The Vatican recommended his removal from the priesthood, but the Indian bishop instead imposed a year in a monastery through a canonical trial, and he continued as a priest in India.

cases.title: India — Andhra Pradesh adoption racket (Tender Loving Care Home)
cases.who: St Teresa's Tender Loving Care Home and other agencies
cases.what: On 22 March 2001 Hyderabad police arrested a man carrying three baby girls allegedly bound for St Teresa's Tender Loving Care Home; other agencies were also flagged. A chargesheet said the home earned Rs 3.33 crore from intercountry adoptions, mainly to the US, in 1999–2001. On 31 August 2005 Sister Teresa Maria Kattikaran and nine others were sentenced to six months' imprisonment for cheating and forgery, and Andhra Pradesh became the first state to bar private agencies from placing children.

cases.title: India — Malaysian Social Services, Chennai: children kidnapped for adoption
cases.who: Malaysian Social Services adoption agency
cases.what: Police suspected the family running the Malaysian Social Services agency since 1991 of kidnapping and trafficking more than 350 children; in May 2005 Chennai police arrested three family members and six others. Children allegedly had their appearance changed and histories fabricated; officers found files for 120 children sent overseas. TIME reported in 2008 that Australian authorities had earlier warnings.

cases.title: India — Preet Mandir, Pune: CBI case on inter-country adoption racket
cases.who: Preet Mandir adoption agency; state officials
cases.what: Preet Mandir placed 518 children in 2004–2006, most abroad, and Frontline reported in 2005 it handled about 7% of India's foreign adoptions while charging high 'donation' fees. CNN-IBN reported in December 2007 that the CBI had confirmed findings on illegal adoptions. On 18 May 2010 the CBI registered a case against a managing trustee and state officials over an alleged inter-country adoption racket.

cases.title: Switzerland — authorities' irregularities in intercountry adoptions (Sri Lanka, India, Tibet…); proposed ban
cases.who: Swiss federal and cantonal authorities; private adoption agencies
cases.what: Swiss authorities soon realised that the placement of children for adoption, often wrongly presented as orphans, was also driven by economic interests and linked to organised child trafficking; decisions were often made on incomplete or falsified documents, and checks on foster families and on legal requirements were insufficient. From the 2010s, under pressure from groups such as Back to the Roots, intercountry adoptions from Tibet, Sri Lanka and India drew public attention. In 2018 the Federal Assembly commissioned a study on intercountry adoption; the Federal Council acknowledged the authorities' irregularities and omissions in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 recommended a general ban on intercountry adoption.

cases.title: Muzaffarpur shelter home — TISS audit and convictions
cases.who: Sewa Sankalp Evam Vikas Samiti (state-funded NGO run by Brajesh Thakur); Bihar Social Welfare Department
cases.what: A social audit of Bihar shelter homes by the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, submitted in April 2018, flagged sexual abuse at the Muzaffarpur girls' home run by Brajesh Thakur's NGO; an FIR followed on 31 May 2018. Medical examination indicated sexual abuse of 34 girls, most of them children. The Supreme Court took up the case and, at the CBI's request, transferred the trial to a POCSO court at Saket, Delhi, because the accused were influential in Bihar. On 20 January 2020 that court convicted Thakur and 18 others; Thakur was sentenced to life imprisonment and has appealed.
cases.cover_up: The then district child protection officer was among the accused; Bihar Social Welfare Minister Manju Verma resigned over the case; the Supreme Court criticised the state for funding the NGO and moved the trial to Delhi. CBI cleared Verma and her husband, a finding disputed by The Caravan.

cases.title: TISS 'Koshish' social audit of 110 Bihar children's homes
cases.who: Children's and girls' homes funded by the Bihar Social Welfare Department, many NGO-run
cases.what: At the Bihar government's request, the Koshish unit of the Tata Institute of Social Sciences visited 110 children's homes in 38 districts and submitted its audit to the Social Welfare Department on 27 April 2018, grading homes as better, administrative negligence or criminal negligence. The Muzaffarpur girls' home run by Sewa Sankalp Evam Vikas Samiti was graded criminal negligence, and the report raised harassment or abuse at 14 other homes, including a girls' home with complaints of severe sexual harassment and violence and homes where children were routinely beaten. The audit triggered the Muzaffarpur FIR of 31 May 2018 and later CBI cases against other Bihar shelter homes.
cases.cover_up: In the audited Bhagalpur home staff refused to give the audit team the key to the complaint box, saying it was lost; the department's director evaded questions about action on the other 14 homes.

cases.title: Deoria shelter home, Uttar Pradesh — girls rescued, CBI case
cases.who: Maa Vindhyavasini Mahila Prashikshan Evam Samaj Sewa Sansthan (NGO); director Girija Tripathi and superintendent Kanchan Lata Tripathi
cases.what: The case came to light when a 10-year-old girl escaped to a women's police station and said girls were taken away in cars in the afternoons and returned crying in the morning. Police rescued 24 girls on 5 August 2018 and sealed the home. Police charge-sheeted the director and her daughter, and seven others in a second FIR. In 2019 the CBI took over and registered cases including sexual harassment, human trafficking, sexual assault and adoption without legal procedure.
cases.cover_up: The UP Women and Child Development Minister said the NGO's recognition had been revoked and funds stopped a year earlier, yet it continued to operate; the government said it would examine who was responsible.

cases.title: Unnao rape case — MLA Kuldeep Singh Sengar
cases.who: Kuldeep Singh Sengar (BJP MLA, Uttar Pradesh)
cases.what: Sengar, then a BJP MLA in Uttar Pradesh, was convicted in December 2019 by a special CBI court in Delhi of raping a minor girl in Unnao district in 2017, and sentenced to life imprisonment; the BJP had expelled him. In December 2025 the Delhi High Court suspended his sentence; on 29 Dec 2025 the Supreme Court stayed that order on the CBI's appeal, and in May 2026 it set the suspension aside, directing the High Court to decide his appeal against conviction within three months or pass a fresh order.
cases.cover_up: The victim's father died in police custody; in July 2019 a truck crash killed two of her aunts and critically injured her and her lawyer (a court later accepted the CBI finding of no foul play in the crash). The arrest came only after the Allahabad High Court ordered it in 2018.

cases.title: Nepal → India — trafficking of girls to Indian brothels (estimates)
cases.who: Trafficking networks recruiting via false job, marriage and online romance offers
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers use job offers and online romance scams to recruit Nepali women and children to India for sex trafficking; Nepali courts convicted 406 traffickers (231 for sex trafficking) in the year. A 2024 study it cites found a majority of workers in Nepal's adult entertainment sector were sex-trafficking victims, nearly half of them children. Research collated on Wikipedia gives estimates of 5,000–10,000 Nepali women and girls trafficked to India each year across a 1,850 km open border.
cases.cover_up: US TIP 2025: serious concerns of official complicity; traffickers bribe some Indian officials to fly Nepali workers to third countries.

cases.title: Bangladesh — girls trafficked to India, Pakistan and the Gulf; Rohingya girls near Cox's Bazar (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers, recruitment agents, armed groups in Rohingya camps
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit Bangladeshi women and girls in sex trafficking abroad, including in India, Pakistan and Gulf countries, and observers estimate children are 40 per cent of Bangladeshi sex-trafficking victims exploited abroad. Tourists have increased demand for sexual exploitation, including of Rohingya girls, near Cox's Bazar, where more than one million Rohingya refugees live in 33 camps. Courts convicted 103 traffickers, down from 407.
cases.cover_up: Corruption and official complicity were significant concerns; corrupt policing in Rohingya camps.

cases.title: India — Kerala priest given double life (Kottapuram diocese)
cases.who: Diocese of Kottapuram
cases.what: On 8 December 2016 a POCSO special court in Ernakulam gave Fr Edwin Figarez double life sentences and a fine of Rs 225,000 for repeatedly raping a 14-year-old girl from January to March 2016 under the pretext of music lessons. Police registered the case on 1 April 2016 after the girl told her mother; he went into hiding and later surrendered.
cases.cover_up: The priest's brother was jailed for helping him hide after the police case was registered; a government doctor who examined the girl was found guilty of failing to report the abuse.

flows.title: Minnesota → India: Fr Joseph Jeyapaul (returned by extradition 2014)
flows.what: Removed from ministry in Minnesota in 2005, he returned to India and continued as a priest; charged in 2006, he was arrested in Erode in 2012 and extradited back in 2014.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2022: Ombudsman (Defensor del Pueblo) report on sexual abuse in the Catholic Church and the role of public authorities, presented to Congress 27 Oct 2023. Survey of 8,013 adults: 11.7% abused before 18; 1.13% abused in religious settings; 0.6% by a Catholic priest or religious; 487 victim testimonies collected
patterns.pattern_summary: Official inquiries into institutional child abuse came in waves: Canada and Ireland first (Hughes, 1989; the Ryan commission, 1999–2009), the United States in 2002–2004, most of western Europe after 2010, Australia's Royal Commission 2013–2017, then France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland from 2021. Where inquiries used population surveys, the numbers were far above church records: about 216,000 minors abused by French clergy and religious since 1950, against about 3,000 identified before. Many "national" studies were commissioned by the church itself. Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, with some of the largest Catholic populations, have no national inquiry in the sources reached.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Daniel Galván, Spanish serial child rapist in Morocco (2013): Pardon revoked after protests; arrested in Spain 7 August 2013 and imprisoned there to finish his sentence. The king had pardoned French child rapist Hervé Le Gloannec in 2006
patterns.pattern_summary: When the accused belongs to another state, a diplomatic service or an army, prosecution depends on that state. UN peacekeepers fall under their own country's courts: at least 134 Sri Lankan soldiers were accused of abusing nine Haitian children in 2004–2007 and none was convicted. The Holy See recalled its nuncio to the Dominican Republic, Józef Wesołowski, and told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow his extradition. South Korea's court refused to send the Welcome to Video operator to the United States. Morocco's king pardoned a Spanish child rapist as a gesture to Spain. Israel's deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments that kept Malka Leifer from extradition for years.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: Spain — children of Republican prisoners taken by the Franco regime. Spain — Dr Eduardo Vela, first 'stolen baby' trial: guilty but not punished.
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children were carried out by states, as policy. Argentina's junta took about 500 babies from detained mothers in 1976–83 (a 2012 court found a "systematic plan"; 140 grandchildren had been identified by July 2025). Under Franco, children were taken from Republican and later unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children into residential schools and non-Indigenous families; Denmark sent Greenlandic children to Danish families in 1951; France moved children from Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported Ukrainian children; the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants in March 2023 for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over it.

cases.title: Spanish Ombudsman report on Church abuse
cases.who: Catholic Church in Spain
cases.what: Spain's first official inquiry into clergy abuse, a nearly 800-page report by Ombudsman Ángel Gabilondo presented to parliament on 27 October 2023 after an 18-month investigation of 487 cases, criticised the church's response as often minimising or denying the problem. A GAD3 survey of 8,000 adults in the report found 1.13% said they had been abused as children by clergy or lay church members and 0.6% by clergy. Gabilondo did not extrapolate a victim count; media applying the percentages to Spain's adult population put the figure at about 440,000 (or about 200,000 for clergy alone). The Spanish bishops apologised but disputed the media figures.

cases.title: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
cases.who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
cases.what: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.
cases.cover_up: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.

cases.title: Spain — Dr Eduardo Vela, first 'stolen baby' trial: guilty but not punished
cases.who: Gynaecologist Eduardo Vela
cases.what: On 8 October 2018 a Madrid court found retired gynaecologist Eduardo Vela, 85, responsible for abducting a newborn, faking a birth and falsifying official documents (the forged birth certificate was dated 1969), but acquitted him because the statute of limitations had run, counting from when the child reached adulthood in 1987. It was the first trial in Spain over the 'stolen babies' of the Franco era and after. A judge had recorded about 30,000 cases of Spanish children taken, according to the report.

cases.title: Romania — post-1989 adoption trade and 2004 ban
cases.who: Private adoption agencies and intermediaries; Romanian authorities
cases.what: After Ceaușescu's fall, television images of about 100,000 children in orphanages led to an adoption boom; private agencies charged €7,500–25,000 and the system 'quickly became awash in corruption' (DW). Romania halted adoptions in June 1991 and, under EU pressure, passed a law in June 2004 banning all foreign adoptions except by grandparents. The European Parliament's rapporteur Baroness Emma Nicholson had criticised 'international adoption and child trafficking' in Romania. Romania's own HCCH return shows 458 intercountry adoptions in 2002, 332 in 2003, 2 in 2005 and 0 in 2006.

cases.title: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
cases.who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
cases.what: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

cases.title: El Salvador — children disappeared by the armed forces during the civil war (Pro-Búsqueda)
cases.who: Salvadoran armed forces
cases.what: Pro-Búsqueda, founded in 1994, has documented close to a thousand children disappeared during the Salvadoran civil war, mostly by the armed forces; many were adopted through flawed procedures to the US, France, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands. On 1 March 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled on the 1982 disappearance of the Serrano Cruz sisters during the 'Guinda de Mayo' military operation. El Salvador created a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children in 2010.
cases.cover_up: The armed forces have not granted access to archives on disappeared children despite years of lobbying.

cases.title: China — intercountry adoption programme ended (2024) after trafficking cases
cases.who: China Center for Children's Welfare and Adoption; state orphanages
cases.what: China opened intercountry adoption in 1992; about 160,000 children were sent abroad, peaking at almost 8,000 to the US in 2005. The programme came to depend increasingly on abuse, abduction and trafficking (New Yorker), including Hunan orphanages buying trafficked babies (2005). On 5 September 2024 the foreign ministry announced the end of the programme, except adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.

cases.title: Spain — children of Republican prisoners taken by the Franco regime
cases.who: Franco regime; Auxilio Social; Women's Protection Board (Patronato de Protección a la Mujer); Falange
cases.what: After the 1936–39 Civil War about 30,000 children were placed in state care under the Franco regime — mostly, in the words of a 2008 ruling by Judge Baltasar Garzón, 'war orphans with parents who were dead, imprisoned, exiled, in hiding, or disappeared'. Children of single mothers held in homes run by the Patronato de Protección de la Mujer were also pressured into adoption. In January 2011 families of 261 babies who disappeared from Spanish hospitals over five decades asked the attorney general to investigate an alleged network of doctors and nurses; lawyers claimed up to 300,000 babies were taken. A 2026 study by forensic geneticists of Spain's National Institute of Toxicology and Forensic Sciences found no evidence of systematic hospital theft and called the 300,000 figure a hoax, while not denying the coercion in Francoist institutions or the 30,000 children placed in state care.
cases.cover_up: Names were changed so children could be given to pro-regime families; the 1977 Amnesty Law has hindered investigation, and many Women's Protection Board files went missing in 1996.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Nigeria — cult-linked networks traffic women and girls to Europe and West African mines (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Nigerian organized trafficking networks, some linked to cult organizations/confraternities
cases.what: The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report says highly organized groups, sometimes linked to Nigerian cult organizations or confraternities, recruit and exploit Nigerian women and girls in sex trafficking in Italy, Spain and the UK, and that networks move women and girls to mining regions in Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire. In the reporting year courts convicted 49 traffickers and the government identified 2,058 victims. It describes corruption and official complicity, including among officials responsible for anti-trafficking, as significant concerns.

cases.title: Morocco — royal pardon of Spanish child rapist Daniel Galván (2013)
cases.who: Daniel Galván Viña
cases.what: Daniel Galván Viña, a retired Spanish professor, was arrested in Morocco in December 2010 and in September 2011 sentenced to 30 years for raping 11 Moroccan children aged 4 to 14. In late July 2013 he was among 48 Spanish prisoners pardoned by King Mohammed VI; after protests outside parliament in Rabat, the king revoked the pardon on 4 August 2013, citing the gravity of the crimes and the victims' rights, and said he had not been told the details of the case. Galván had already left Morocco; he was later arrested in Spain.
cases.cover_up: King Mohammed VI pardoned Galván on 30 July 2013 among 48 Spanish prisoners; he left Morocco on an expired passport with authorities' knowledge before the pardon was cancelled. Protesters in Rabat were violently dispersed. A 2010 US cable reported a 2006 royal pardon of a French man convicted of abusing a 15-year-old boy in Marrakesh.

cases.title: Romania — girls in state institutions at risk; victims sent across Europe (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers; staff of some government-run institutions
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says most identified victims are women and girls exploited in Romania and in Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK; children in government-run institutions, particularly girls in homes for persons with disabilities, are at risk of sex trafficking; and Roma children as young as 11 are 'sold' into marriage. Courts convicted 161 traffickers (143 for sex trafficking) and 600 victims were identified in 2024.
cases.cover_up: Alleged complicity, misconduct and negligence by government employees in cases involving children in government-run homes remained a concern.

patterns.pattern: Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones
patterns.role: Mission or crisis zone where children were abused
patterns.role_note: MONUC peacekeepers — sexual exploitation of girls in Bunia (OIOS 2004). Ebola response, North Kivu & Ituri — Independent Commission on SEA by WHO and other responders. Also home country of accused personnel: DR Congo → CAR: MINUSCA FARDC contingent allegations (offenders).
patterns.pattern_summary: Children in war zones and camps were abused by the people sent to protect or feed them. A 2002 UNHCR and Save the Children report documented aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food for sex with children. In Haiti, more than 100 Sri Lankan peacekeepers were sent home in 2007 over the abuse of children; none was convicted at home. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014–2016. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators in the WHO-led Ebola response in Congo (2018–2020), 21 of them WHO staff, with victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly allegation counts since 2004.

patterns.pattern: War and the taking of children
patterns.role: Abductions and sexual violence by armed groups
patterns.role_note: LRA Makombo massacre and abductions, DR Congo (2009). DR Congo — UN-verified sexual violence and abduction of children by M23, FARDC and armed groups (2024). Bosco Ntaganda (UPC/FPLC, Ituri) — ICC conviction incl. rape and sexual slavery of child soldiers. Thomas Lubanga (UPC, Ituri) — ICC's first conviction: conscription and use of children.
patterns.pattern_summary: In war, taking children is often a tactic. The UN commission on Syria found in 2016 that ISIS sold Yazidi girls in markets as sexual slaves and that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls at Chibok in 2014; 82 were still captive a decade later. The International Criminal Court convicted the LRA commander Dominic Ongwen on 61 counts, including forced marriage and sexual slavery. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, with girls as young as eight. cases.title: Ebola response, North Kivu & Ituri — Independent Commission on SEA by WHO and other responders
cases.who: WHO staff and contractors, Ministry of Health and partner personnel in the 10th Ebola response
cases.what: The Independent Commission appointed by WHO reported on 28 September 2021 that it identified 83 alleged perpetrators, 21 of whom were established with certainty as WHO employees during the response; most were Congolese staff hired temporarily who used their authority to obtain sex, often in exchange for jobs. The review team heard 63 women and 12 men aged 13 to 43; the youngest, a girl selling phone cards in Mangina in April 2019, said a WHO driver raped her. Nine rape allegations were recorded and 29 women and girls became pregnant.

cases.title: MONUC peacekeepers — sexual exploitation of girls in Bunia (OIOS 2004)
cases.who: UN Organization Mission in the DRC (MONUC) military contingents, military observers and civilian staff
cases.what: After media and Congolese women's reports in March and May 2004, OIOS investigated in Bunia from May to September 2004. It found that sexual contact with peacekeepers occurred 'with regularity', usually in exchange for food or small sums of money, and that many cases involved girls under 18, some as young as 13. Of 72 allegations reported to MONUC, many could not be investigated because they were non-specific; six cases were fully substantiated. The findings led to the Secretary-General asking Prince Zeid Ra'ad Al-Hussein of Jordan to prepare the 2005 comprehensive report on SEA by peacekeepers.

cases.title: MINUSCA peacekeepers — rapes near Bambari airport
cases.who: MINUSCA contingents believed by survivors to be from the Republic of Congo or DR Congo
cases.what: Human Rights Watch documented eight cases of sexual exploitation and abuse by MINUSCA peacekeepers during research in Bambari in January 2016, including a 14-year-old girl and an 18-year-old woman who said they were gang-raped near Bambari airport. Most incidents occurred between September and December 2015, when a Republic of Congo contingent guarded the airport.

cases.title: MINUSCA — DR Congo battalion repatriated after child abuse allegations
cases.who: Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) battalion serving with MINUSCA
cases.what: About 800 troops from the Democratic Republic of the Congo served with the UN mission in the Central African Republic (MINUSCA) in 2015. In August 2015 three Congolese peacekeepers were accused of raping three female civilians, including a minor. In January 2016 MINUSCA confirmed the Congolese unit would withdraw and not be replaced, after a UN review of its equipment, vetting procedures and preparedness; it was not clear whether the abuse allegations were the main factor. cases.title: Lord's Resistance Army — child abduction and sexual slavery; ICC conviction of Dominic Ongwen

cases.what: The LRA abducted tens of thousands of children in northern Uganda for use as fighters, porters and 'wives'; UNICEF estimated at least 25,000 by 2006. cases.title: LRA Makombo massacre and abductions, DR Congo (2009)
cases.who: Lord's Resistance Army commanders Lt. Col. Binansio Okumu ('Binany') and 'Obol', reporting to Gen. Dominic Ongwen (per HRW)
cases.what: From 14 to 17 December 2009 Lord's Resistance Army forces attacked at least 10 villages in the remote Makombo area of Haute-Uélé, north-eastern DR Congo, killing at least 321 civilians and abducting 250 others, including at least 80 children. Human Rights Watch, which documented the previously unreported massacre after a field mission in February 2010, said it was carried out by two LRA commanders who reported to Gen. Dominic Ongwen, the senior LRA leader believed to command its forces in Congo and wanted by the International Criminal Court.

cases.what: The UN verified sexual violence against 358 girls in the DRC in 2024, by M23 (68), CODECO (63), the Armed Forces of the DRC (47), Raia Mutomboki (33), Nyatura (24) and others, and the abduction of 815 children, by ADF (265), M23 (178) and others. cases.title: Bosco Ntaganda (UPC/FPLC, Ituri) — ICC conviction incl. rape and sexual slavery of child soldiers
cases.who: Union of Congolese Patriots (UPC) / Patriotic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (FPLC)
cases.what: On 8 July 2019 ICC Trial Chamber VI found Bosco Ntaganda guilty of 18 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Ituri in 2002–2003, including rape, sexual slavery and the conscription and use of children under 15; he was the first person convicted of sexual slavery by the ICC. He was sentenced to 30 years on 7 November 2019, confirmed on appeal on 30 March 2021. He had told child soldiers, 'When you're a soldier, you get a woman for free'.

cases.title: Thomas Lubanga (UPC, Ituri) — ICC's first conviction: conscription and use of children
cases.who: Union of Congolese Patriots (UPC/FPLC)
cases.what: On 14 March 2012 the ICC found Thomas Lubanga guilty of enlisting and conscripting children under 15 and using them in hostilities, and sentenced him on 10 July 2012 to 14 years; the verdict was confirmed on 1 December 2014. Sexual violence against girl soldiers was raised at trial but not charged. He was released on 15 March 2020 after serving his sentence.

cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says mining bosses, other miners, family members, government officials and armed groups force or coerce adults and children into forced labour in artisanal mines in eastern DRC, including through debt bondage, and that most trafficking is internal, including sex trafficking and forced marriage of girls.
cases.cover_up: Traffickers named in the report include government officials; corruption and complicity contributed to impunity.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 3,263 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman).
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption moved from one sending country to the next as each was exposed. The map colors each sending country by whether it was later closed or suspended and draws 59 documented flows.

cases.title: Nigeria — Aba 'baby farm': 32 pregnant girls freed
cases.who: Cross Foundation clinic proprietor
cases.what: In late May 2011 Abia State police raided the Cross Foundation clinic in Aba and rescued 32 pregnant girls, mostly aged 15–17, allegedly held so their babies could be sold for illegal adoption or ritual use; four babies already sold were recovered. The proprietor was arrested, according to police commissioner Bala Hassan. Nigerian police had uncovered a network of 'baby farms' posing as orphanages in Enugu in 2008, and more were found in later years (five in 2013, eight in 2015 per Makinde et al.).

cases.title: Nigeria — Lagos raid: 162 children rescued from 'baby factory' and unregistered orphanages
cases.what: In April 2018 Lagos State Commissioner for Youths and Social Development Agboola Dabiri said 100 girls and 62 boys had been rescued from a 'baby factory' and two unregistered orphanages; some had been sexually abused. The BBC noted babies from such places can be sold for adoption, child labour or trafficking, and that in 2013 17 pregnant teenagers and 11 babies were rescued from a house in Imo State.

cases.title: Chibok schoolgirls abduction — Boko Haram
cases.who: Boko Haram (JAS)
cases.what: On the night of 14 April 2014 Boko Haram gunmen raided the dormitories of the Government Girls Secondary School in Chibok, Borno state, and loaded 276 girls onto trucks; more than 50 escaped within hours, mostly by jumping off the lorries, leaving 219 in captivity, some later found in the Sambisa Forest. Amnesty International said on the tenth anniversary in April 2024 that 82 girls remained in captivity and that 20 released girls had been forced to marry former Boko Haram fighters; in April 2015 it estimated that at least 2,000 women and girls had been abducted by the group since the start of 2014.

cases.title: Dapchi schoolgirls abduction — ISWAP/Boko Haram
cases.who: Boko Haram faction (ISWAP)
cases.what: On the evening of 19 February 2018 militants stormed Dapchi, Yobe state, and abducted girls from a boarding school; Nigeria's government said 110 schoolgirls were missing. On 21 March 2018 the government said 106 children — 104 schoolgirls, a girl who did not attend the school and a boy — had been freed, and denied paying a ransom. Five girls were reported to have died during the journey after the abduction. The only Christian girl in the group, who refused to convert, remained in captivity.

cases.title: Kankara schoolboys abduction (Katsina, 2020)
cases.who: Armed bandits; Boko Haram's Shekau claimed responsibility
cases.what: On the night of Friday 11 December 2020 heavily armed gunmen raided the all-boys Government Science Secondary School in Kankara, Katsina state, where more than 800 students lived. The military said 333 pupils were unaccounted for. In an audio message a man identifying himself as Boko Haram leader Abubakar Shekau claimed the abduction; Nigerian officials attributed it to bandits, and the BBC later described a local gang leader as the mastermind of the kidnapping of about 300 boys. The boys were freed within about a week.

cases.title: Nigeria — UN-verified abduction and forced marriage of children by JAS and ISWAP (2024)
cases.who: Jama'atu Ahlis Sunna Lidda'Awati Wal-Jihad (JAS/Boko Haram), ISWAP, Bakura
cases.what: The UN verified the abduction of 991 children (354 boys, 637 girls) in Nigeria in 2024 by JAS (690), ISWAP (294) and Bakura (7), most for recruitment and use. It also verified sexual violence, all involving forced marriage, against 419 children (7 boys, 412 girls) by JAS (304), ISWAP (114) and Bakura (1). In 2023 the UN had verified sexual violence against 366 children following abduction.

cases.title: Ogoshi brothers — Nigeria-based sextortion of a Michigan teenager
cases.who: Samuel and Samson Ogoshi, Lagos (convicted); Ezekiel Ejehem Robert (charged)
cases.what: Men in Lagos used hacked Instagram accounts, posing as a girl, to obtain explicit images from a 17-year-old in Michigan and demanded $1,000; he died by suicide in March 2022. A federal grand jury indicted the brothers in November 2022; they were extradited from Nigeria in August 2023. The indictment said they tried to extort more than 100 people. They pleaded guilty to conspiracy to sexually exploit teenage boys (announced 10 April 2024) and were each sentenced to 17.5 years in September 2024. A third defendant, Ezekiel Robert, appealed a Nigerian extradition order; charges against him remain pending.

cases.title: Nigeria — cult-linked networks traffic women and girls to Europe and West African mines (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Nigerian organized trafficking networks, some linked to cult organizations/confraternities
cases.what: The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report says highly organized groups, sometimes linked to Nigerian cult organizations or confraternities, recruit and exploit Nigerian women and girls in sex trafficking in Italy, Spain and the UK, and that networks move women and girls to mining regions in Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire. In the reporting year courts convicted 49 traffickers and the government identified 2,058 victims. It describes corruption and official complicity, including among officials responsible for anti-trafficking, as significant concerns.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers away and received them
patterns.role_note: Verona → Mendoza: Fr Nicola Corradi; Phoenix → Rome: Joseph Henn (fugitive 2003–2019).
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, brother, teacher or headmistress was found abusing children, the institution often moved them rather than calling the police: to another parish, another school, another state, or another continent. The map draws 34 documented moves recorded by inquiries, courts and the institutions' own files, and colors every country that sent or received an abuser. The Pennsylvania grand jury found bishops moved abusers between parishes; Bishop Mulkearns knew of Gerald Ridsdale's offending by late 1975 and kept reappointing him to new parishes; the Adass Israel School paid for Malka Leifer's 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel before police were told; the Makin review called John Smyth "a problem solved and exported to Africa".

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: No national inquiry. "There are no official statistics"; under the Lateran concordat the Italian Bishops' Conference said in May 2012 its priests have no obligation to report suspected abuse to police; victims group Rete l'Abuso has demanded an independent external inquiry for years
patterns.pattern_summary: Official inquiries into institutional child abuse came in waves: Canada and Ireland first (Hughes, 1989; the Ryan commission, 1999–2009), the United States in 2002–2004, most of western Europe after 2010, Australia's Royal Commission 2013–2017, then France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland from 2021. Where inquiries used population surveys, the numbers were far above church records: about 216,000 minors abused by French clergy and religious since 1950, against about 3,000 identified before. Many "national" studies were commissioned by the church itself. Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, with some of the largest Catholic populations, have no national inquiry in the sources reached.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Lateran concordat and Italian reporting (2012): —
patterns.pattern_summary: When the accused belongs to another state, a diplomatic service or an army, prosecution depends on that state. cases.title: Romania — post-1989 adoption trade and 2004 ban
cases.who: Private adoption agencies and intermediaries; Romanian authorities
cases.what: After Ceaușescu's fall, television images of about 100,000 children in orphanages led to an adoption boom; private agencies charged €7,500–25,000 and the system 'quickly became awash in corruption' (DW). Romania halted adoptions in June 1991 and, under EU pressure, passed a law in June 2004 banning all foreign adoptions except by grandparents. The European Parliament's rapporteur Baroness Emma Nicholson had criticised 'international adoption and child trafficking' in Romania. Romania's own HCCH return shows 458 intercountry adoptions in 2002, 332 in 2003, 2 in 2005 and 0 in 2006.

cases.title: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
cases.who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
cases.what: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

On 1 March 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled on the 1982 disappearance of the Serrano Cruz sisters during the 'Guinda de Mayo' military operation. El Salvador created a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children in 2010.
cases.cover_up: The armed forces have not granted access to archives on disappeared children despite years of lobbying.

cases.title: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
cases.who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
cases.what: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. cases.title: Switzerland — authorities' irregularities in intercountry adoptions (Sri Lanka, India, Tibet…); proposed ban
cases.who: Swiss federal and cantonal authorities; private adoption agencies
cases.what: Swiss authorities soon realised that the placement of children for adoption, often wrongly presented as orphans, was also driven by economic interests and linked to organised child trafficking; decisions were often made on incomplete or falsified documents, and checks on foster families and on legal requirements were insufficient. From the 2010s, under pressure from groups such as Back to the Roots, intercountry adoptions from Tibet, Sri Lanka and India drew public attention. In 2018 the Federal Assembly commissioned a study on intercountry adoption; the Federal Council acknowledged the authorities' irregularities and omissions in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 recommended a general ban on intercountry adoption.

cases.title: Switzerland — 'Kinder der Landstrasse': Yenish children removed by Pro Juventute (1926–1973)
cases.who: Pro Juventute foundation, with federal and cantonal authorities
cases.what: From 1926 to 1973 the Pro Juventute foundation's 'Hilfswerk für die Kinder der Landstrasse' (Charity for the Children of the Country Road) took around 600 Yenish children from their families and forcibly placed them in homes or foster families; around 2,000 children of the Swiss Traveller community are believed to have been affected by such measures overall. The persecution depended on authorities at every level of government, which were closely intertwined with Pro Juventute in personnel and co-funded the Hilfswerk. On 20 February 2025 the Swiss government, taking note of a legal opinion led by Professor Oliver Diggelmann, acknowledged that the persecution of Yenish and Sinti people was a crime against humanity under current international law (but not a 'cultural genocide'), and reaffirmed its apology. (Care agent covers Verdingkinder.)

cases.title: Swiss administrative detention and forced placements (incl. Verdingkinder)
cases.who: Swiss cantonal and municipal authorities; about 650 institutions
cases.what: The Independent Expert Commission on Administrative Detention, set up under the Federal Act of 21 March 2014, presented its final report on 2 September 2019. It found more than 60,000 people were interned in about 650 institutions without court order, mainly from 1930 to 1981, and that victims were abused physically, psychologically and sexually. The Swiss government had apologised in 2010; a 2016 law created a CHF 25,000 'solidarity contribution' for victims of compulsory measures, including children placed as indentured farm labourers (Verdingkinder).

cases.title: Landslide Productions / Operations Avalanche and Ore
cases.who: Landslide Productions (payment portal, Thomas and Janice Reedy)
cases.what: Landslide, a Fort Worth, Texas portal run by Thomas and Janice Reedy, processed credit-card sign-ups for third-party sites, some offering child abuse images. US agents raided it in August 1999; a jury convicted Thomas Reedy, who was sentenced to 1,335 years (reduced to 180 on appeal), and Janice Reedy got 14 years. US Operation Avalanche examined about 35,000 names on the database, and the FBI passed details of 7,272 British residents to UK police, starting Operation Ore, Britain's biggest computer crime investigation; raids began in May 2002. CEOP said 140 children had been rescued in the UK. Later forensic examination showed large-scale credit card fraud in Landslide's records (54,348 sets of stolen card details), and some people were wrongly accused; a legal challenge in 2009 argued that many convictions for incitement rested on flawed credit-card evidence. Follow-on operations took place in other countries.
cases.cover_up: Later reconstruction of the Landslide data found many listed names were victims of credit-card fraud, and the validity of UK Operation Ore procedures was questioned; an estimated 33 suicides followed in the UK.

cases.title: John Smyth — Iwerne camps, Zimbabwe and South Africa (Makin Review)
cases.who: Iwerne Trust (evangelical camps), Church of England; Zambesi Ministries (Zimbabwe); Anglican Church of Southern Africa

cases.title: Bosnia — trafficking of women and girls; IPTF monitors and SFOR/DynCorp contractors
cases.who: Traffickers and bar owners; local Bosnian police; UN International Police Task Force (IPTF) monitors; US SFOR civilian contractors (DynCorp)

A US Army CID report documented DynCorp contractors buying women from brothels; one confessed to buying a woman (with an Uzi) for 1,600 Deutschmarks. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad from 1953 to 2008; its Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in 2025 that the state was responsible for human rights violations in those adoptions. Romania (1990s), Guatemala (until 2007–08), Cambodia and Vietnam, Nepal, Ethiopia (banned 2018) and others followed, each closed after inquiries found children bought, stolen or registered as orphans. Receiving countries then began to look at themselves: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after the Joustra committee, and China ended it in 2024. The map colors each sending country by whether it was later closed or suspended and draws 59 documented flows.

patterns.pattern_summary: The map's documented record is thickest where people looked. Childlight's 2026 update rests on representative surveys from only 60 countries; South Asia, West and Central Africa and the Middle East and North Africa lack them. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied 2023 data. In 2025, 14% of the 23.4 million reports to the US CyberTipline could not be placed in any country, and North Korea had 12. Countries with large churches and many children's institutions, such as Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, have held no national inquiry into institutional abuse in the sources reached. Where a country is colored only by estimate on this map, this is why.
